text: The only long walk in the whole area that I could do with a two year old and a pushchair. Flat the entire way, benches every fifty metres, and I never once had to carry anybody. There are no toilets anywhere, which cost us an urgent detour.

Walked from the Gateway to the very end and back, which is longer than it looks. At seven it is completely full and there is a football match happening somewhere. Go at six in the morning and you have it to yourself.

Flat and paved and completely level, which is what we needed. The sea wind was strong enough that we gave up after thirty minutes and took a taxi back. No shelter and no toilets, so it is a fair-weather walk only.
The view from the park above is the one worth having. From the road you are standing in the middle of the thing you came to see. Get there for seven because the lights come on in stages.

The steps up to it defeated my husband entirely and we were told the vehicle route is rough and unlit. We went back down to the road and stood in the traffic instead, which was worse. If you cannot manage steps, do not attempt this from the seaward side.
Great photograph, and about two hundred people all taking the same photograph. Twenty minutes is the honest amount. The parapet is the only place you can stand and it fills up first.
Sunday only and gone by one, so time it early. Flat lane, no bags to carry at the entrance, and my daughter chose a book instead of a toy, which I did not expect. Pricier than a real flea market.
Good records and genuinely old books, but the lane is shoulder to shoulder by half past ten. Browse, do not plan to find anything specific. I bought a book and stood in a crush for twenty minutes.
Six studio doors open at once on a Friday and you can walk in and look. We spoke to two of the six. Flat lane, quiet, and a cafe at the end if you want to sit. Not a gallery, more a walk.
We came on a Tuesday at midday and four of the six doors were shut. The lane itself is worth a walk and the work is good, but check the day before you plan around it.

We were the only people there at quarter past six. Two joggers, one fisherman and the sky. Flat, free, and a genuine half hour of quiet at the far end of the walk. My wife cried at the sunrise, which is her business.
The same spot at nine on a Saturday with fifty people and a yoga class is a completely different place. Worth doing at dawn and not worth doing at nine.

The promenade path is separated from the road the whole way, so my eight year old rode behind me on the towpath and neither of us was stressed. Child seat was available when I asked. Ninety minutes covers a lot and it is flat enough to stop anywhere.
Hybrids were good and the ride is easy, but the wind off the water is a hard effort for anybody who is not fit, and there is nowhere to stop and shelter halfway. Toilets at the hire point only.

I needed forty minutes to sit by myself and not buy anything and this is the only place in four areas where that is possible. Six stone benches, tree cover, a wall, no traffic. Nobody looked at me once.
My husband sat for an hour and I joined him for twenty minutes. Flat, paved, shaded, benches with backs. The only problem is that there is no toilet, so we did not stay the morning.

You are paying for the view and the food is very good rather than the reason. Booked three weeks ahead. The noise from the promenade below is part of it and after nine it gets loud, so I would sit upstairs.
Took clients here and it worked, but the two hour minimum at lunch means this is never a ninety minute plan, and the lift is the only way up, which is a bottleneck at peak.

My five year old made one and lit it herself and carried it home on the train. There is a stool for children at the bench, which is the detail that made it work. The room is stacked with finished ones in October.
We went in January with no warning and there was nothing festive about it, just lanterns. Still a pleasant hour. Check the month before you book it as a Diwali activity.

I am seventy four and I have done this class four times now. Half the people on the mat are older than me and nobody minds if you watch from the bench for the first ten minutes, which I do. Free, on the flat, and the sea in front of you.
Mats ran out so we stood at the back on the paving and it was fine. Go at half six not at seven. Lovely, gentle, and nobody performs it at anybody.
Eighty rupees for a cut pav bhuna and a chai, standing on the pavement, and it was the right answer when we had twenty minutes and no budget. No seating and no card machine, so carry cash.
We ate standing at a pavement cart in our good coats and did not enjoy the standing part at all. The bhuna was excellent. For a short stop with nowhere to sit, fine, otherwise look for benches.

I have shot for ten years and I still learned something about what happens to highlights when you drop the shutter. Six people, one tripod each, and he does not let you touch the camera until you ask.
I took a phone because that is all I had and I could not do a single thing we were taught. Forty minutes and I contributed nothing. The description says camera with manual mode and it means it.

It was pouring and this arcade was the reason we did not have to cancel the day. Dry stone floor, pillars, benches, and my son watched the rain through the gaps for forty minutes. Level the whole way, which is rare on this coast.
Shelter is the point and it delivers, but in a proper cloudburst about a hundred other people are under there too, and it gets tight near the steps. Still better than the alternative.
Step-free from the street to the terrace, chairs with arms, and a toilet we were allowed to use which is more than the promenade offers. The terrace is covered so we sat out while it rained.
Sensible and well run and the coffee is expensive for what it is. Nobody will remember it. That is fine if what you need is a dry table with a view and a toilet nearby.

The planting is genuinely good and the gaps between the buildings catch the harbour. It is hot and broken and everyone says avoid it. Go early, take water, and do not pretend the paving is a footpath, because it is not.

Hundreds of steps, broken slabs, and no working toilets. My husband gave up after the second terrace and we sat on a wall for twenty minutes instead. The views are lovely and I would not send anybody who cannot manage steps.

Eight buildings in a hundred minutes, all on flat paving, finishing exactly as the lights came on. The guide knew which reclamation each building was on and made eight hundred years of landmaking make sense. Booked a week ahead.
Very good guide, and there is no toilet at any point on a hundred minute walk, which I had not thought about. It started raining at forty minutes and we had nothing to do but stand there.

Plastic chairs, cracked pavement, and every stall is better than it looks. This is the row opposite the hotels, not the hotel stretch, and it is a third of the price. Smells like frying and the sea is two metres away.
Sitting on a plastic chair on a broken pavement for ninety minutes is not what my hips needed, and there is no toilet anywhere near. The food was very good and we will not do it again.

No laptops after noon is a rule and it means the room stays calm and the people in it are talking to each other. Excellent filter coffee and a cake that sold out by two. The front room is level, the courtyard has two steps.
Charming and quiet and there is no toilet, which for a two hour sit-down is a problem. The courtyard is lovely but two steps, so we had the front room, which is fine.

I am sixty nine and have not drawn since school. Twelve of us, folding stools for anyone who cannot stand, and a tutor who did not correct me once in an hour. Six hundred rupees for that is remarkable.
Lovely idea and flat ground, but four of us standing at an easel for an hour on hard paving is harder than it sounds, and the seats are backless. Bring something to sit on.

This is the answer to taking three small children to the sea. Fenced, flat, ride-on toys for the two year old and balance bikes for the older two, and a shaded bench right beside it for me. There are toilets next door, which is the part I did not expect to find.
My three year old loved it and my wife found it noisy and cramped at six o clock. The staff were kind. Go at four rather than six when everybody else has arrived.

The last section before the river mouth where the crowd thins out and the water changes colour. Cooler than the middle of the promenade and about ten people instead of two hundred. Natural end to a walk rather than a place to start one.
The paving here has been washed out and I lifted my son over two bad sections. The evening is the best time for everyone else, so a pram is a bad idea and the description should be blunter about it.

Small room, small prints, and the artist was working while we looked, which is much better than a shop. He will print something for you and it arrives a week later. Flat, and there is nothing else on the lane.

Much better than plastic chairs on the pavement. Order from the carts, sit at a proper bench at the sea wall, take the plate back. The children could sit properly, which they cannot on the seawall itself.
Benches rather than chairs, which after an hour is not ideal, and still no toilet to be found. Service at the shared counter was quick and kind, and the view is the best thing about it.
